reference.source: Oxford Textbook of Endocrinology and Diabetes
clinicalPearls: Tumour-induced osteomalacia is a rare acquired paraneoplastic syndrome caused by FGF23, and other phosphatonins, secreted by usually small benign phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours of the mixed connective tissue variant.
Excess FGF23 produces renal phosphate wasting, hypophosphataemia and low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, with normal calcium and PTH.
Adults present insidiously with bone pain, muscle weakness, fatigue, height loss and fragility or insufficiency fractures, and are frequently misdiagnosed for years.
The biochemistry mirrors X-linked hypophosphataemia but is acquired in adulthood with no family history; a raised or inappropriately normal intact FGF23 supports the diagnosis.

Tumours are often tiny and hidden in the extremities, craniofacial bones or sinonasal tract, so localisation depends on functional imaging; 68-gallium DOTATATE PET/CT is the most sensitive, supplemented by MRI.
Complete surgical resection is curative, with rapid normalisation of phosphate; incomplete localisation is the main obstacle to cure.
When the tumour cannot be found or resected, medical therapy with oral phosphate and active vitamin D, or burosumab, controls the biochemistry.
Consider this diagnosis in any adult-onset hypophosphataemic osteomalacia without a hereditary or nutritional explanation.
reference.pathophysiology: Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours secrete fibroblast growth factor 23 (and less commonly other phosphatonins such as sFRP4 and MEPE). Circulating FGF23 downregulates the proximal tubular sodium-phosphate cotransporters, causing renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphataemia, and suppresses renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase so that 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is inappropriately low. The resulting chronic hypophosphataemia impairs mineralisation of osteoid, producing osteomalacia. Because the tumours are typically small, slow-growing and anatomically obscure, the phosphaturic state persists and drives progressive skeletal disease until the lesion is identified and removed.
additionalDifferentials: X-linked or other hereditary hypophosphataemia presenting late
additionalInvestigations: serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and PTH
whole-body MRI and selective venous sampling for FGF23 if required
redFlags: failure to localise a strongly suspected tumour
rare malignant phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour with metastases
reference.prognosis: The condition is curable with complete tumour resection, after which symptoms and biochemistry resolve, although localisation may take years and rare malignant variants carry a worse outlook.
pitfalls: prolonged diagnostic delay from attributing symptoms to osteoporosis or fibromyalgia
not measuring phosphate and FGF23 in unexplained bone pain
relying on anatomical imaging alone and missing small tumours
assuming a drug cause is excluded once the agent is stopped without rechecking phosphate
incomplete resection leading to biochemical recurrence
references: Oxford Textbook of Endocrinology and Diabetes
management: Complete surgical resection of the FGF23-secreting phosphaturic mesenchymal tumour, which reverses the biochemistry and heals the osteomalacia
Oral phosphate replacement together with active vitamin D (alfacalcidol or calcitriol) while the tumour remains occult or after incomplete resection
The anti-FGF23 antibody burosumab as an alternative targeted treatment when the tumour cannot be localised or removed
Localisation with functional gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/CT supplemented by whole-body MRI and, if needed, selective venous FGF23 sampling
Physiotherapy, analgesia and fracture prevention for bone pain and proximal myopathy
Surveillance for secondary hyperparathyroidism and nephrocalcinosis during long-term phosphate and vitamin D therapy
Multidisciplinary metabolic bone and surgical care
